source_sentence_cues.text: Could our universe be inside a black hole?
It's a personal side-interest — not part of the lab's research programme.
We read the original papers to see what they actually predict.
One idea gives us a number to check against real stars.
For galaxy spin, the sources give no expected size for the effect — and even a perfect measurement couldn't tell us a black hole was the cause.
So this route closes.
The idea is not declared true or false.
Here's the first surprise.
We found at least five different proposals under this label — black-hole universe, or BHU for short.
A closed universe inside a black hole.
A collapse that bounces instead of crushing to a point.
A universe that inherits its parent's spin.
Universes that reproduce, tuning the numbers built into physics.
And baby universes with entirely different fingerprints.
Five ideas — and no shared prediction.
We wrote what we found into a closing record — the document this video reports from.
To test an idea, the model has to risk being wrong.
It needs a number, a range, or a distinctive pattern that a measurement can miss.
And if you find it, it has to point back at that one idea — not at three different ones.
In the whole family we surveyed, the closing record found one clean numerical test.
It uses neutron stars—the ultra-dense collapsed cores of exploded stars.
The ones we can time as they spin are called pulsars, and their mass can be measured.
One proposal — called cosmological natural selection — says universes have children: every black hole buds off a new universe with slightly different physics.
Over many generations, that would tune physics toward making black holes.
In the Brown–Lee–Rho chain our record surveyed, the Brown–Bethe maximum neutron-star mass is about one and a half times the mass of our Sun—one point five solar masses.
Their paper says a neutron star at approximately two solar masses or above would put that chain in ‘serious doubt or simply falsify’ it.
That's a real test — a number that could be proven wrong.
Weighing a star thousands of light-years away is hard, so every measurement comes with an uncertainty range.
Two heavy pulsars matter here.
One weighs in at one point nine seven Suns, give or take point zero four — just under two.
The other: two point zero eight, give or take point zero seven.
At the sixty-eight point three percent level the paper quotes, that one clears two Suns.
At the stricter ninety-five point four percent level, the closing record says it does not.
Here we have to be careful.
Brown, Lee, and Rho gave two possible readings, joined by an ‘or’: a heavy neutron star would put the chain in serious doubt, or simply falsify it.
The closing record does not decide which side applies — and neither does this video.
The finding is narrower: observations have entered the regime named by the source.
A different proposal led to our sky work.
If the parent black hole rotates, the child universe inherits its axis.
The source says galaxies should tend to align with that axis.
It then says clockwise- and counterclockwise-spinning galaxy counts should be different.
Our search wasn't chasing a phantom.
The claim really is there in the paper — in words.
What's missing is any number to go with it.
But that sentence was added in 2025, after the galaxy studies cited as support.
It was not a prediction made before the data—this one came after.

The paper gives equations for spinning systems, but not a numerical forecast for galaxy handedness: no expected size, no rule for where or when it should be stronger, no independently predicted direction, and no range that would count as a hit or a miss.
Suppose a controlled survey found a real spin-handedness difference.
That would be interesting.
But that broad observation would not identify BHU by itself.
The same lopsided sky could come from several different causes.
Without a fingerprint only a black-hole birth would leave, the measurement can't pick one.
A successful measurement is not automatically a successful test of this model.
The route therefore fails in two independent ways.
There's no pass-or-fail range to grade a measurement against — the idea never says how big the effect should be.
And without a unique signature, a positive result cannot identify BHU.
We could build a trustworthy measurement and still be unable to answer the BHU question.
The hunt had a source.
It did not have a target.
What would change the verdict?
First, a published calculation that says how big the spin difference should be — with a pass-or-fail range.
Or second, a fingerprint only a black-hole birth would leave—not merely the broad fact of spin asymmetry.
A confirmed spin asymmetry alone would still not test BHU.
This route reopens only when a BHU model supplies a calibrated target or a unique signature.
